questions.q: Per this lesson, which of the following is one of the six standard sections of an integration design document?
options: Page layout assignment
Org-wide default sharing setting
Lightning component bundle structure
Error handling — what happens on failure, retry policy, and how a failed record gets resolved
questions.explain: The six standard sections are pattern, direction, endpoints/authentication, data mapping, error handling, and volume/frequency. Error handling specifically covers what happens on failure and how it gets resolved.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say a fire-and-forget integration pattern needs specific documentation of how the publisher would learn about a downstream failure?
options: Because fire-and-forget integrations are never used in real Salesforce architectures
Because by design, the publisher doesn't wait for a response, so nothing automatically tells it something went wrong unless the design explicitly documents how that gets surfaced
Because fire-and-forget always guarantees delivery and failures are impossible
Because fire-and-forget patterns require a sequence diagram in every case
questions.explain: A fire-and-forget publisher doesn't wait for or receive a response by design — so unless the integration documentation explicitly addresses how a downstream failure would ever be detected, that gap goes unaddressed.

questions.q: What should an architect check regarding a Platform Events-based event-driven integration, per this lesson?
options: Whether events are held indefinitely for an offline subscriber the same way some other messaging systems queue messages
Whether the org has fewer than ten custom objects
Whether the Apex callout uses GET or POST
Whether the ERD includes a legend
questions.explain: The lesson specifically notes that an event-driven design built on Platform Events needs documentation of subscriber behavior if a subscriber is down when an event publishes, since events are not held indefinitely for an offline subscriber the way some queued-messaging systems hold messages.

questions.q: What practical test does this lesson give for deciding whether an integration needs a sequence diagram instead of just prose and a table?
options: Every integration always needs a sequence diagram, with no exceptions
If two different readers could reasonably draw two different pictures of 'what happens, in what order' from the prose alone, a sequence diagram is needed to remove the ambiguity
A sequence diagram is only needed for batch integrations, never for real-time ones
A sequence diagram is needed only when more than one external system is involved, regardless of complexity
questions.explain: The test is practical and about ambiguity: when order and timing are complex enough that prose could be read two different ways, a sequence diagram is the fix — a simple single-call scenario, as in this lesson's worked example, doesn't need one.

questions.q: In the worked inventory-check example, where is the OAuth client secret for the external inventory system stored, per this lesson's documented approach?
options: Directly in the integration design document, for completeness
Hardcoded in the Apex callout class
In a Named Credential, which stores the endpoint and authentication details separately from code and is never put into the documentation itself
In the Integration_Error_Log__c custom object
questions.explain: The worked example explicitly uses a Named Credential to hold the OAuth client credentials, stating that the actual secret is never placed in code or in the documentation — only the fact that a Named Credential is used is documented.
